opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is one of those questions that sounds deep but actually has a pretty practical answer. We regulate plenty of things we don't fully understand. We didn't have a complete theory of combustion chemistry when we started writing building codes and fire regulations. We regulated pharmaceuticals long before we understood the molecular mechanisms of most drugs. What you need for regulation isn't a perfect philosophical definition. You need observable proxies that correlate with the risk you care about.

And with AI, we actually have decent proxies. Compute is the obvious one. The amount of compute that goes into a training run is measurable, it's concentrated in a small number of data centers, the chips come from a tiny number of manufacturers. It's not a perfect measure of capability, but it's a pretty good one, and it's something you can actually audit. You can also look at capabilities directly: can this system autonomously replicate, can it help someone synthesize a pathogen, can it find and exploit software vulnerabilities at scale? Those are concrete, testable things. I don't need to resolve what consciousness or general intelligence "really is" to know that a system that can do those things is dangerous.

Honestly, I think the "we don't know what intelligence is" argument often functions as a kind of rhetorical delay tactic. It sounds humble and scientific, but the implication is that we should let a handful of companies race ahead building increasingly powerful systems until philosophers reach consensus, which will be never. That's backwards. The uncertainty is an argument for more caution, not less. If you don't understand the thing you're building, and it's getting more powerful every year, that's exactly the situation where you want guardrails.

So my view is: start with what's measurable, put limits on the frontier, require real accountability from the people building these systems, and update as our understanding improves. That's how we've handled every other powerful technology we've managed not to blow ourselves up with.

r001.rationale: The response says regulation does not require a perfect definition of intelligence and offers measurable proxies, distinguishing difficulty from impossibility.

r002.rationale: It gives combustion and pharmaceutical examples, but does not compare the issue to tobacco companies demanding identification of a cancer-causing chemical before smoking regulation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most common objections I hear, and I think it's kind of a category error. The idea that you need to have a precise, philosophically complete definition of a thing before you can regulate it, that's just not how regulation has ever worked for anything.

We don't have a rigorous definition of "health," but we have the FDA. We don't have a settled theory of what "money" fundamentally is, and yet we have central banks and securities law. Nobody at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission can give you a complete, from-first-principles account of what a "safe" reactor is, but they can tell you that this particular design with these particular failure modes isn't allowed to get built next to a school. Regulation is almost never about the essence of a thing. It's about behaviors, capabilities, and consequences.

So when people say, "Well, we can't regulate intelligence because we can't define it," my response is: good news, you don't have to. You don't regulate intelligence. You regulate systems. You regulate compute. You regulate what people are allowed to deploy, what kind of testing has to happen before deployment, who's liable when something goes wrong. These are all extremely concrete, measurable things. You can count GPUs. You can measure training runs in FLOPs. You can ask, did this system pass evaluations for whether it can help someone synthesize a pathogen? These are not metaphysical questions.

And honestly, I'd flip it around. The fact that we don't understand what intelligence is, that we don't understand what's going on inside these systems, that's not an argument against regulation. That's the strongest argument for it. If I came to you and said, "I'm building something very powerful, I can't tell you how it works, I can't predict what it will do, and I can't explain what it even is," you would not say, "Well, I guess we'd better not have any rules then." You'd say, "Maybe slow down until you can answer some of those questions."

The demand for a perfect definition before we act is, in practice, a demand for inaction. And in a situation where the systems are getting more capable every six months, inaction is itself a choice, and it's not a neutral one. So I'd say: start with what's measurable, start with the things that are obviously dangerous, build the institutions that can actually do oversight, and let the philosophy catch up. It always has before.

r001.rationale: The response says a precise definition of intelligence is unnecessary for regulation, which can instead target systems, capabilities, and consequences.

r002.rationale: It gives other comparisons, such as health, money, and reactor safety, but does not compare the demand to identify a cancer-causing chemical in tobacco smoke before regulating smoking.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate two questions: what intelligence actually is, and what these systems can do. We don't need to solve the first question before we can do anything about the second. We don't have a perfect definition of life, but we can still regulate biological experiments.

If a system can help someone develop a dangerous weapon, or autonomously break into computer systems, that's something you can investigate and regulate. You don't have to first establish whether it's “really intelligent.” You care about the capability, who has access to it, and whether anyone can reliably control it.

Of course, we don't know how to measure all of this properly yet. That's a serious problem. But uncertainty isn't a reason to just keep building increasingly powerful systems and putting them out into the world. It's a reason to demand more evidence of safety, to have independent oversight, and to be able to stop when we don't understand what we're doing.

So I'd frame the question less as “Can we define intelligence?” and more as “What should a company have to demonstrate before it gets to expose everyone else to this risk?”

r001.rationale: The response says we need not settle what intelligence is before regulating AI capabilities, so difficulty defining intelligence does not make regulation impossible.

r002.rationale: It compares AI regulation to regulating biological experiments despite uncertainty about the definition of life, but does not mention tobacco companies or identifying a cancer-causing chemical in smoke.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think you need a complete definition of intelligence to regulate AI. You need to understand enough about what a system can do, what risks it creates, and who’s responsible when something goes wrong.

If someone builds a system that can autonomously carry out dangerous actions, the relevant question isn’t, “Is this really intelligent?” It’s, “Can you control it? Can you demonstrate that it won’t cause unacceptable harm?” Those are practical questions, even if the underlying science is incomplete.

And uncertainty cuts both ways. If we don’t understand these systems very well, that isn’t automatically an argument for letting people deploy them without constraints. It can be a reason to demand stronger evidence of safety. We should be honest that our tests will be imperfect, but we don’t have to solve intelligence philosophically before we can hold developers accountable.

r001.rationale: The response says a complete definition of intelligence is unnecessary for regulation and frames regulation around practical risks, distinguishing difficulty from impossibility.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare the issue to tobacco companies demanding identification of a cancer-causing chemical before smoking regulation.
